title: How to check if an investor is legit
summary: How to check if an investor is legit: verify the fund, the person, the email domain and the portfolio. Sixtyfour researches each one and cites every source.
body_markdown:
Check the fund, the person, the email domain and the portfolio separately, then check that they connect. A real investor works at the fund they name, writes from that fund's own domain, and is named by companies the fund has backed. Find the fund's website and phone number yourself, never through the message, and stop if anyone asks for a fee before any money arrives, or for special software to join a call.


Find its website through a search, read its team and portfolio pages, and date its domain in ICANN's Lookup tool. In the US, look for it on the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure site and on EDGAR, where a Form D includes the names and addresses of the filer's executive officers, and outside the US look up its management company in the national registry. Then confirm a few portfolio investments in the companies' own announcements and with founders you reach yourself.


Yes. A fee before the money arrives, for diligence, legal work, a valuation or an escrow account, is the pattern in the fake investor cases public reporting describes. The Justice Department prosecuted one case in which dozens of start-ups paid about $380,000 in "due diligence fees" to someone with no financial ability to invest, and an FBI warning about schemes built on fictitious bank instruments lists being asked to pay an advance fee before funding among their common features. Confirm any request with the fund on a number from its own website.


Find the fund's website yourself and compare its domain with the one in the email, one character at a time, looking for a dropped or doubled letter, an extra word such as capital or partners, or a different ending. Date the domain in ICANN's Lookup tool, since a fund with a long history rarely writes from a domain created last month. Then write to the partner at the address on the fund's own website, or call its main number, and ask.


A fake investor scam is an approach from someone posing as an investor, often using a real fund's name and a real partner's identity, who offers to back a company and then asks the founder for money or access before any investment. Requests in public reporting include a refundable diligence fee, a commission in cryptocurrency and installing special software for a call. The investment never arrives.


Yes. Sixtyfour is a research agent that takes an investor's name, email address and claimed fund, researches where the person works today, which domains the fund uses and whether the companies the fund has backed name it, and returns each finding with its source and a confidence score, for the whole result or, when you ask for it, for each field. Anything it could not establish is reported as open, and you decide what to do.


Stop replying, send no money or documents, and do not open further links or attachments from them. Tell the fund whose name was used, report the profile to the platform the approach came through, and file a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center, which asks for one regardless of the amount lost. If you have paid, contact your bank at once and ask it to recall the payment.
